catalog_quote: Brainard 1991 p.190: 'There are nineteen phonemes in Upper Tanudan Kalinga: fourteen consonants and five vowels. ... Word stress and consonant length are also phonemic. There are two syllable patterns: CV and CVC.' SIL fact sheet: 'Stress is phonemic, but is marked only in the dictionary.' Olson et al. 2008 p.143: 'two adjacent identical consonants represent a long consonant. We write them as two consonants in order to allow for stress to be marked properly on forms such as item 33: abobba [abobˈba] ‘short’. Second, two adjacent identical vowels represent two distinct vowels occurring in separate syllables, such as in item 20: poos [ˈpoos] ‘few’.' Wordlist p.144: '2. you sing.; thou sika [ˈsiʔa] 3. he siya [siˈja] ... 6. they dida [diˈda]'.

new_statements.quote: There are 19 phonemes in Upper Tanudan Kalinga: 14 consonants and 5 vowels. The consonants are /p,t,k,b,d,g,m,n,ng,s,l,w,y/ and glottal stop. The vowels are /i,u,o,e,a/. Stress and consonant length are also phonemic. There are two syllable patterns: CV and CVC.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Tanudan Kalinga has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so this is the first stress statement held by the project: it establishes only that stress is phonemic (contrastive), not where it falls. It describes the Upper Tanudan variety (ISO change request 2011-079 merged [kgh] Upper Tanudan into [kml] Tanudan Kalinga, so it falls under lowe1412), whereas the listed 1977 dictionary is for Lower Tanudan.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive (phonemic) in Upper Tanudan Kalinga; the sketch gives no placement rule, no examples of minimal pairs, and no statement of which syllables can bear stress. Consonant length (gemination) is likewise phonemic.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the phonology appendix is a one-page sketch and says nothing further about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The listed work (SIL 81029, 1977) is a Lower Tanudan Kalinga dictionary. The only phonology statement actually read (Brainard 1985, Appendix C p. 124) is explicitly about Upper Tanudan Kalinga; SIL tags that work with subject language Tanudan Kalinga [kml], and Glottolog lists it under lowe1412 because the 2011 ISO change request 2011-079 merged Upper Tanudan [kgh] into Tanudan Kalinga [kml]. So the 'stress is phonemic' reading rests on the Upper Tanudan variety and should be labelled as such on the site; no statement for Lower Tanudan was obtained.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every quoted passage is verbatim at the stated locator in the copies we hold (Brainard 1991 p.190; SIL fact sheet first spelling rule; Olson et al. 2008 pp.143-144). sources.quote: 'There are 19 phonemes in Upper Tanudan Kalinga: 14 consonants and 5 vowels. The consonants are /p,t,k,b,d,g,m,n,ng,s,l,w,y/ and glottal stop. The vowels are /i,u,o,e,a/. Stress and consonant length are also phonemic. There are two syllable patterns: CV and CVC.' No positional or weight rule anywhere in the fetched pages; the Introduction (p.vii) has no phonology content.
